extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, federal equity masters/referees, and judges (also law students studying patent procedure)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and procedural-substantive standards governing evidence, proof, exceptions, recommittal, and the master's report in equity patent suits when an accounting of profits or damages is referred to a master.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff must furnish sufficient testimony to enable computation
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff must furnish sufficient testimony to enable the master to arrive at definite conclusions, and cannot rely upon him to suggest what proof may be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff cannot leave it to the master to fill gaps — must present the evidence needed for specific computations of profits or damages (cases: Brady v. Atlantic Works; Garretson v. Clark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Master must receive and collate all relevant and material evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The master must receive all relevant and material evidence, and by collating and comparing it must ascertain the data for his computation, and formulate their result in the award of a specific sum as damages or profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Master's role is investigative and computational: gather, compare, compute and award a specific monetary amount based on the evidence presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff may compel defendant presence and production of books, but must segregate infringing items
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff may compel the presence of the defendant and the production of his books and subject them to examination, but if the books disclose the sale or use of various articles, some of which may not have been covered by the patent, the plaintiff must by other testimony separate those by which his rights have been infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production of voluminous/commingled records requires plaintiff to supply additional proof to allocate sales/use to infringing items (cases cited: Garretson v. Clark; National Car Brake Shoe Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion of accounts does not excuse segregation of infringing goods
rubrics_metrics.description: The confusion of accounts is not a confusion of the goods sold; as some may infringe while others do not, those which do must be separated by evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where accounting records are confused, the plaintiff must separate infringing from non-infringing goods by proof (National Car Brake Shoe Co. v. Terre Haute Car & Mfg. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Master's accounting period not limited to date of decree
rubrics_metrics.description: In taking the account the master is not limited to the date of entering the decree, but may extend it down to the time of hearing before him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Master may compute profits/damages up to the master hearing date (cases: Rogers v. Reissner; Rubber Co. v. Goodyear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence must be positive and certain; opinions have little weight
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence must be positive and certain. The opinions of witnesses concerning the value of the invention to the defendant, or the amount of injury to the plaintiff, are of little weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court requires concrete proof (sales records, costs, etc.); mere witness estimates are weak (multiple cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlements or license fees paid by others generally do not show defendant's profit or plaintiff's loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of sums paid in settlement or as license fees by other parties does not tend to show the profit made by the defendant, nor the loss suffered by the plaintiff, unless the settlement was voluntary on both sides and for an exactly similar infringement, or unless the license fee is universally established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such comparators are admissible only in narrow, comparable circumstances (cases: Rude v. Westcott; Corley v. Marckwald; United Nickel Co. v. Central Pacific R. R. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant may show amounts he expended for other processes performing same work
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount which the defendant has himself expended for other processes or instruments performing the same work or effecting the same saying as the patented invention, is a fair measure of its worth to him, and may therefore be proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant can introduce proof of alternative process costs to mitigate profit/damage claims (cases: Munson v. City of New York).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions in the answer and their evidentiary effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissions in the answer as to the extent on the accounting are bound to suggest what proof is needed, and may be considered by the master, but the plaintiff must still furnish enough to show the profits or damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissions narrow proof issues but do not replace the plaintiff's burden (cites: Garretson v. Clark and others).

rubrics_metrics.name: License-fee evidence: apportionment when only some claims infringed
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a license fee is established with reference to the entire patent, and only certain claims are infringed, the master must apportion the license fee according to the value of the claims, if possible, unless the remaining claims are merely structural; burden of proof on plaintiff to show value of infringed claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Master must try to allocate an established license fee to the infringed claims rather than applying it whole-cloth when only some claims are at issue (cases: Willimantic Thread Co. v. Clark Thread Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Master must determine whether license fee is fair measure if infringement pre-dates fee
rubrics_metrics.description: The master must determine whether a license fee is the fair measure of the value of the invention where the infringement took place before the license fee was established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if later license fees exist, master assesses applicability to earlier infringements (Wooster v. Thornton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence on open methods and degree of advantage admissible on profits question
rubrics_metrics.description: On the question of profits, evidence to show what open methods there are and their degree of advantage is admissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of competitive/operational advantages (open methods) is relevant to assessing profits due to infringement (Black v. Thome).

rubrics_metrics.name: Master may examine defendants, inspect books and machinery; personal examination permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: The master, taking an account, may examine the defendants and inspect their books; the master may also make a personal examination of the apparatus at the request of the parties, and such examination will not be reversed if done in their presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hands-on inspection by the master is proper and carries probative weight if parties participated (Piper v. Brown).

rubrics_metrics.name: All papers and objections during master hearing filed with master, not in court; objections must be taken contemporaneously
rubrics_metrics.description: During the hearing the case is pending before the master and all papers must be filed with him and not in court. Objections to the evidence presented must be taken to him as the evidence is offered; although he has no power to finally decide upon them, he must note both the objection and his ruling, to be reviewed later by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To preserve review rights, objections must be made to the master at time evidence is offered and recorded in his minutes (practice repeated in multiple cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: After draft report is filed no additional evidence can be received
rubrics_metrics.description: After the draft report is filed no evidence can be received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The draft report marks the close of evidence before the master (cases: Piper v. Brown; Holmes).

rubrics_metrics.name: No evidence may be introduced after master submits a draft report to a party
rubrics_metrics.description: No evidence can be introduced after the master has submitted a draft of his report to one of the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submission of draft to parties freezes the evidentiary record before the master (Piper v. Brown; Piper/Brown notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to master's draft and final report: timing and preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions to the final report cannot be made on any question which was closed by the decree referring the case to the master, nor on any ruling as to the admissibility of evidence unless the objection was duly entered on the record and was urged before the master after the filing of his draft report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should raise and preserve objections early (take exceptions to draft report; note admissibility objections before master) or they will be barred on review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulings of master not ordinarily reviewed by court pending reference
rubrics_metrics.description: The rulings of the master, except in extreme cases, will not be reviewed by the court pending a reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not seek piecemeal review of master's rulings during the reference unless exceptional circumstances; follow normal exception procedure (cases cited: Bate Refrigerating Co. v. Gillette; Welling v. La Bau).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception-taking procedure before a master
rubrics_metrics.description: An exception should always be taken on the spot to each ruling of the master which a party intends to contest; it need not then be drawn up in form, but it should be taken by giving notice to the master, and it is his duty to note the facts in his minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt oral notice to master suffices to preserve issues; later formal exceptions will be based on those minutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: If master reports evidence at request, court reviews facts; otherwise court reviews only law
rubrics_metrics.description: If the master reports the evidence at the request of one or both parties, the court, if there be proper exceptions, will review the questions of fact as well as law; but if the evidence is not reported, the court does not review the facts but simply re-examines questions of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requesting the master to report evidence preserves factual review by the court on exceptions (practice in this circuit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to master's report must point out defects and cite record evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions must point out the defects in the report, and must direct the attention of the court to those portions of the evidence of the record in which they appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic or unsupported exceptions will be overruled; counsel must identify the specific errors and record locations (cases: Turrill v. Illinois Central R. R. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions of fact by master generally not reviewable unless all testimony is presented
rubrics_metrics.description: The conclusions of the master concerning matters of fact cannot be reviewed, unless the entire testimony is presented to the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain review of factual findings, arrange for full evidence to be reported (cases: Piper v. Brown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may recommit report for further hearing or amendment for substantive errors
rubrics_metrics.description: The court has power to recommit the report to the master for a further hearing, or for an amendment, when it is erroneous in principle, or when the master takes a wrong view of the invention, or when it fails to complete the computation, or exhibits any other misconception in law or fact which an additional investigation may correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommittal is available for material legal/factual/calculation errors but not to permit a party to raise waived objections or introduce testimony previously omitted (cases: Steam Stone Cutter Co. v. Windsor Mfg. Co.; Faulks v. Eamp).

rubrics_metrics.name: Findings of master will not be set aside unless against weight of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings before a master are of nearly the same solemnity as those before the court, and his finding will not be set aside unless against the weight of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High deference is afforded to master's factual findings; overturn only on strong showing (Tilghman v. Proctor cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report may be set aside or corrected by court where legal or factual error appears and correction is possible
rubrics_metrics.description: A report awarding a substantial sum, but showing on its face that no account of damages or profits which can be taken will be legally sustainable, may be set aside. When the report or the accompanying evidence discloses both the error and the means for its correction, the court may rectify the mistake without a recommittal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If error and corrective means evident, court can correct; otherwise recommit for further inquiry (examples cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Master's report acceptance leads to final decree with monetary award and equitable relief
rubrics_metrics.description: The acceptance of a report of the master in favor of the plaintiff is followed by a final decree awarding him the sum found by the master as damages or profits, or both, and granting a perpetual injunction or such other equitable relief as may be necessary; where several plaintiffs exist, the decree provides for distribution proportioned to interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance is dispositive and converts the master's computation into a final enforceable decree (procedural consequences spelled out).

rubrics_metrics.name: Master's draft and final report timeline: duty to consider objections and file final report
rubrics_metrics.description: Having submitted his draft report to the parties and having heard their objections and reconsidered his conclusions, the master may file his final report at any time without an order from the court; parties have a right to file exceptions to the final report founded upon previous objections made to the draft report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Master should (and customarily does) allow time after draft for objections, consider them, then file final report; exceptions should be grounded in objections to draft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections to admissibility preserved by motion to suppress where evidence not finally allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence as to allowances not finally allowed is properly taken by the master and must be objected to by a motion to suppress the testimony, not by exceptions to the master's report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evidence is improperly received but not included in final allowance, use appropriate motions (American Nicholson Pavement Co. v. City of Elizabeth).

rubrics_metrics.name: If master takes wrong view of invention or report lacks necessary base data, court will send back for further evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the master takes a wrong view of the invention, and so mistakes the profits, the report will be sent back for further evidence. When the master's report shows the percentage of profit but not the amount on which the percentage should be calculated, the case must be sent back for further evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports omitting essential factual foundation or misinterpreting the invention will be recommitted to obtain the missing proof or correct the view (cases: Ruggles v. Eddy; Gonow v. Mers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and scope of appeal to U.S. Supreme Court from final decree
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors of law or fact committed by Federal courts of equity are corrected by an appeal to the Supreme Court of the United States. This appeal lies only on a final decree dismissing the bill, or awarding damages or profits or other relief to the plaintiff after acceptance of the master's report; motions for appeal must be made within two years, and if the appeal is to operate as a supersedeas the motion must be made within sixty days with sufficient security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent cases can be appealed without respect to amount; procedural time and security rules apply for supersedeas effect (statutory and case citations provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Final decree may be amended only during same term; decree need not follow master's findings on merits
rubrics_metrics.description: A final decree can be amended only during the term at which it was entered. Although an interlocutory decree is given for the plaintiff, yet if on the return of the master's report it appears that he ought not to recover, the final decree may depart from both and dismiss the bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court retains ultimate authority to differ from master's findings and interlocutory relief; final decree has limited amendment window.
